newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-PICTURE TELLS A STORY OF MILAN V SAMPDORIA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-PICTURE TELLS A STORY OF MILAN V SAMPDORIA.

text.p: For a true picture of Sampdoria's rivalry with Milan, tear your eyes away from the superb panorama of the Italian Riviera at the Genoa club's Bogliasco headquarters, and focus on the huge silver engraving in the entrance hall.
The image, measuring five metres by two, captures the defining moment of Samp's only league championship in 1990/91 - Brazilian Cerezo's winner at the San Siro against Milan.

"It's still known as the most beautiful goal in serie A history," says Sampdoria historian Piero Sassarego. "Five different players touched the ball as it danced through the air never hitting the ground, before Cerezo's volley."
Today, this historic picture freeze-frames the golden era of Sampdoria - the late 1980s and early 1990s.
At that time, Milan, with Dutch trio Marco van Basten, Frank Rijkaard and Ruud Gullit, not to mention Arrigo Sacchi's revolutionary tactics, were European thoroughbreds.
Sampdoria, then the youngest club in the world's best first division, were the all-Italian answer to Milan.
With old-fashioned catenaccio defensive tactics, Vujadin Boskov's Samp hit their opponents on the counter-attack through the "terrible twins" - Roberto Mancini and Gianluca Vialli.
From 1985, when Sampdoria won their first major trophy, the Italian Cup, against Milan at the San Siro, the clubs vied to dominate Italian soccer for seven years.
As Milan won two consecutive European Cups, Sampdoria reached successive European Cup Winners' Cup finals, winning the second in 1990 against Anderlecht.
And while Samp claimed three Italian Cups, Milan were twice crowned Intercontinental champions and European Supercup winners.
Milan claimed their 11th league title in 1988, but Sampdoria were always close behind, finally pushing their rivals into second place in 1991.
"Sampdoria was the true anti-Milan," Sassarego says, "not Juve, Inter or Napoli."
Today, the Bogliasco picture not only captures the essence of Samp's rivalry with Milan, it neatly frames the changing fortunes in the clubs' recent histories.

Of the Sampdoria players from that match, only Mancini is still with the club. In contrast, most of the Milan players watching Cerezo score are still with the team - Franco Baresi, Alessandro Costacurta and Paolo Maldini, not to mention manager Sacchi.
Sampdoria might be 47 years younger than Milan, but their 35-year-old president Enrico Mantovani - the youngest in serie A - can still teach his seniors a lesson about renovation.
Inheriting the club from his petrol broker father Paolo, Enrico decided Genoa, with a population of 700,000, did not have the resources to support an expensive football team.
In the past two seasons, with the help of coach Sven-Goran Eriksson, he has off-loaded Ruud Gullit, Atilio Lombardo, Pietro Vierchowod and England's David Platt.
In their place, the Swede has brought in talent from the youth team like Marco Carparelli and Emanuele Pesaresi and foreigners like Pierre Laigle and Argentina's Juan Veron.

The strategy has reaped rewards on and off the pitch. Samp are second in the league, four points behind leaders Juventus, while their bank balance is an estimated 15 billion lire ($9.3 million) in the black.
It's says much about the Milan side that meets Sampdoria on Sunday that they have 37-year-old Vierchowod, a former Samp defender, in their squad.
The team that vied with Sampdoria for the championship and took four league titles and a European Cup in five years under Fabio Capello is past its sell-by date.
Languishing 10th in serie A, seven points behind Sampdoria, the club has tried to go back to the future by replacing Uruguayan manager Oscar Washington Tabarez with Sacchi.
But Milan's glorious past - 36 Italian and European titles - is slipping away from them and Sacchi wants a purge.
Such is Milan's decline that on Sunday, Sampdoria will start favourites on a ground where they have won just twice in 10 years and seven times since the club's first meeting in 1947.
It's a measure of Samp's rapid coming of age that when they were formed in 1946, Milan already had three league titles.
At the time, Sampdoria's city rival Genoa, Italy's oldest club, was Milan's chief rival.
Sampdoria was an amalgamation of two Genovese clubs - Sampierdarenese and Andrea Doria - invited by Italy's federation to form a team to rival the historic Genoa side.
The team was based in the Sampierdarenese suburb of Genoa known as the "Manchester of Italy" for its heavy industry.
Ironically, Samp was popularly known as "Milan's old boots" with half its players signed from Internazionale or AC Milan.
In 1979, after relegation to serie B, the club was taken over by the late Paolo Mantovani, who after six years put a title in the trophy room - the 1985 Italian Cup.
Samp's golden age peaked in 1992 when they reached the European Cup final, losing to Barcelona. Eighteen months later, Cerezo had retired, Vialli had moved to Juventus and Mantovani had passed away.

Sampdoria's first victory at Milan since Cerezo's famous strike would not only keep the Genoa side in the hunt for their second league title. It might also put Milan in the picture about the secrets of rebuilding ageing teams.
